'''''Panicum capillare''''', known by the common name '''witchgrass''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=PACA6|taxon=Panicum capillare|accessdate=30 January 2016}}</ref> is a species of [[Poaceae|grass]]. It is a [[native plant]] to most of North America from the [[East Coast of the United States|East Coast]] through all of the [[West Coast of the United States|West Coast]] and [[California]]. It can be  found as an [[introduced species]] in [[Eurasia]], and as a [[weed]] in [[garden]]s and [[landscaping|landscaped]] areas.<ref>[http://www.ppws.vt.edu/scott/weed_id/panca.htm Virginia Tech Weed Profile]</ref> It grows in many types of habitat.

==Description==
''Panicum capillare'' is an annual [[bunchgrass]] growing decumbent or erect to heights exceeding one meter (3 feet). It is green to blue- or purple-tinged in color. In texture it is quite hairy, especially on the [[leaf|leaves]] and at the nodes. The [[ligule]] is a fringe of long hairs.

The [[inflorescence]] is a large open [[panicle]] which  may be over half the total length of the plant, up to half a meter long. At maturity it fans out, spreading to a width over 20 centimeters. As the plant dies and dries, the panicle may break off whole and becomes a [[tumbleweed]].<ref>[http://herbarium.usu.edu/webmanual/info2.asp?name=Panicum_capillare&type=treatment Grass Manual Treatment] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110611160748/http://herbarium.usu.edu/webmanual/info2.asp?name=Panicum_capillare&type=treatment |date=June 11, 2011 }}</ref>

''Panicum capillare'' has been proposed as a solution to herbicide-contaminated soil, showing an uptake of atrazine in testing,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Murphy |first1=Ian J |last2=Coats |first2=Joel R |date=2011-03-01 |title=The capacity of switchgrass ( Panicum virgatum ) to degrade atrazine in a phytoremediation setting |url=https://academic.oup.com/etc/article/30/3/715/7762740 |journal=Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry |language=en |volume=30 |issue=3 |pages=715–722 |doi=10.1002/etc.437 |pmid=21154841 |bibcode=2011EnvTC..30..715M |issn=0730-7268}}</ref> and growing readily in the same soils as agricultural crops.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Clements |first1=David R. |last2=Stephen J. Darbyshire |first2=Antonio DiTommaso |last3=Cavers |first3=Paul B. |last4=Sartonov |first4=Alison D. |date=January 2004 |title=The biology of Canadian weeds. 127.
